meta.title: The ChatGPT Answer, Triaged
meta.description: What the mis-scoped oracle answer is actually worth, where each piece applies, and what it cannot help with

props.title: The ChatGPT Answer, Triaged
props.subtitle: We asked about the grammar. It answered about command authority. The answer is still worth money — in the right lane.

props.content: What happened: the export tool auto-picked the wrong files (dispatch and FMM code instead of the parser), so ChatGPT answered a question we didn't ask. But the question it DID answer — how commands should carry authority to the flight management module — is a real open lane for us, and its answer is competent. This page extracts the value: a one-paragraph thesis, a plain-words read of each of its ten steps, the one recommendation that is already red on our test panel today, and the hard boundary of what it cannot help with.

props.label: SCOPE
props.title: What we asked vs what it answered
❓ What we asked
props.content: Why does the template grammar need perfect text — where should robustness to garbled speech-recognition output live? (Parser internals: phonetic matching, repair pricing, lattice decoding.) This question is now re-exported properly: the full-context zip bundle with the entire engine, all template rows, and 535 measured perfect-vs-garbled transcript pairs.

props.title: 💬 What it answered
props.content: How the system should decide which parsed facts become executable authority for the flight management module — and how to stop that authority from being invented in scattered code heuristics. A six-month roadmap in ten small steps, each with its own do-not-build list. Wrong question. Genuinely useful answer for the command-authority lane.

props.label: THE THESIS
props.title: Its core idea in one paragraph

props.content: The parser records what was HEARD. A small typed catalog decides which of those facts become executable authority. Everything else rides along as context that can never be executed, matched, or sent over the wire.

Today, when a controller says 'proceed on course', the value the flight management module receives is the free-text string 'on course' stuffed into a route field — a magic value some downstream code has to know about. The answer's fix: the parser keeps recording the words as heard, but what goes to the FMM is a typed value from a declared list — route_action = proceed_on_course. Every executable parameter gets this treatment: a declared name, a declared set of legal values, and a hard rejection for anything outside it.

Its strongest structural point: authority is currently INVENTED in several code paths (default-metadata fallbacks, proposal heuristics, row overrides, and scorer fallbacks that quietly treat parser slots as expected authority). Each of the ten steps moves one phrase family from 'code invents the value' to 'the catalog declares it' — and deletes the code path that did the inventing in the same change.

props.label: THE TEN STEPS
props.title: Each step in plain words, with my read
props.subtitle: My verdicts are triage reads — each step still gets a ratchet-audit before anyone executes it

rows.plain: Two different harness files independently work out what the FMM was 'supposed' to receive, and on compound turns they can fall back to parser slots — quietly grading the FMM against the parser's own output. Make ONE shared resolver that validates against the catalog first.
Replace the magic string route='on course' with a typed value. Smallest possible bead; copies the pattern of the already-landed resume_own_navigation.
'Climb via the SID' is an action, not a number. Give altitude_action a declared enum instead of leaning on the numeric altitude field.

read.text: Adopt later — needs corpus case audit

rows.plain: A squawk command carries exactly one executable value: the four-digit code. Nearby frequency talk in the same breath must not leak into it.

read.text: Partially exists — verify, small gap if any

rows.plain: 'Taxi to the ramp, this frequency' currently smuggles the symbolic value 'this_frequency' into the numeric frequency field. Type it as its own action value.

read.text: Adopt — matches a known taxi-row debt

rows.plain: Numeric speed is the only executable value; 'reduce'/'increase' stay as spoken facts unless the FMM actually needs them.
On 'taxi via Alpha, hold short runway 31': the taxi command owns the route, the hold command owns the runway, and neither inherits the other's leftovers. Prove it on one corpus family.

read.text: Adopt — aligns with our compound-turn failures

rows.plain: A code heuristic currently synthesizes BOTH a free-text condition AND a typed event for 'advise clear of weather'. Keep only the typed event as authority.
Emergency type is currently created by a generic metadata fallback. Move it to explicit contract rows without touching the P0 confidence/source gates.

read.text: Later — touchy lane, gates must stay intact

rows.plain: For one batch of multi-command turns, write down explicitly what the parser AND the FMM should each produce — then delete the fallback that guessed. This is the endgame of step 1.

read.text: Adopt last — directly targets our 10 fmm_decision reds

props.content: Two things make this roadmap trustworthy rather than consultant noise. First, every step names what NOT to build — no route ontologies, no state machines, no nested payloads, no scorer 'tolerance' settings. That matches our own gate law. Second, every step is one phrase family, landed atomically with its corpus gold and tests — the same one-slice-per-packet shape we already work in.

props.label: THE DIRECT HIT
props.title: It named the thing that is red right now

props.content:
The answer's foundation is 'value domains': for every parameter a command can carry to the flight management module, a policy file declares what values are legal — runway means a number 1 through 36 with an optional L, C, or R; anything else is rejected outright, never clamped or guessed. We ALREADY HAVE this file (the command-parameter contract) and a census test that walks every gold scenario and fails the moment a parameter appears with no declared domain.

That census is the one red light on our infrastructure panel today. The eleven gold corrections we landed this week introduced two parameter names the corpus had never used: 'fix_or_distance' (a position report can be anchored at a named fix OR a distance — 'report 5 miles out') and 'parking' (a taxi clearance can end at a parking spot). Neither has a declared domain yet, so the gate went red at introduction time — which is the gate doing its job, not a regression. The fix is two policy entries: legal values plus an FAA grounding reference each.

props.title: Why this matters
props.content: The oracle independently re-derived the exact mechanism our own gate law already enforces. When an outside model and our own hard-won rules converge on the same design, that part of the roadmap is low-risk to execute.

props.label: THE BOUNDARY
props.title: What this answer cannot help with

props.content:
None of the ten steps touches our biggest measured loss: the grammar parses perfect transcripts flawlessly (476/476) and loses heavily on real speech-recognition output — 'CLEARED TOUCH AND GEO' for touch-and-go, 'STRAIGHT AND' for straight-in. That is a parser-internals problem: how words are matched, how repairs are priced, whether we parse the recognizer's alternatives instead of its single best guess.

That question is what the new export answers-in-waiting is for: the zip bundle with the complete engine, every template row, the kill-test findings (so it can't re-propose the four dead ends), and the measured confusion pairs. Same oracle, correctly scoped this time, with the off-topic fence written into the prompt.

props.title: Two lanes, two oracles, no crossover
props.content: Command-authority lane: THIS answer is the roadmap — ten beads, adopt selectively, ratchet-audit each. Grammar/ASR lane: pending the bundle answer — nothing from this answer applies there. Keeping the lanes separate is the whole lesson of the mis-scoped export.

props.label: VERDICT
props.title: What to actually do with it
✅ Keep
props.content: The whole answer, as the command-authority lane's working roadmap. Its first two moves — the shared expected-FMM resolver and the proceed_on_course bead — are small, high-value, and match failures we can already name. The two missing value domains get fixed regardless; that red predates the answer.

props.title: ⚠️ Gate
props.content: Nothing executes from prose. Each adopted step becomes its own packet with pinned thresholds, a ratchet-audit of its file claims (it guessed some paths from partial context), and the usual zero-movement baseline gate. Step 9 (emergency) waits — the P0 confidence and source gates in that lane are not to be touched casually.

props.title: 🗑️ Discard
props.content: Nothing outright — but its file-by-file table and gate matrix are its weakest sections (written from incomplete visibility). Treat those as hints, not authority. Our own baseline family and infra panel remain the only gate truth.
